sources.scope: Standard tasks, analysis scripts and data from 40 young adults for seven ERP components (N170, MMN, N2pc, N400, P3, LRP and ERN), with recommended electrode sites (Table 1) and measurement windows (Table 2) to choose before analysing new data.

sources.scope: Walks through the visual and auditory ERP component sequence (Table 1 maps components to processes) and gives working rules on baselines, trial counts, eye movements, measurement, referencing, refractoriness and offsets.
sources.title: A brief introduction to the use of event-related potentials in studies of perception and attention

guidance.t: Show at least 100 ms of prestimulus baseline in figures and check that baseline differences are clearly smaller than the effect of interest.
Plan trials per condition per participant by component: C1 over 1,000; P1 and N1 300–1,000; N2pc about 250; P3 about 35–60.
Jitter the intertrial interval so alpha does not phase-lock to the stimuli, and keep participants alert, because alpha grows when they are sleepy or bored.
Exclude trials with blinks and eye movements rather than relying only on correction; record EOG, and use an eye tracker when absolute fixation matters.
Keep stimulus manipulations orthogonal to attention manipulations so physically different stimuli do not masquerade as attention effects.
Measure amplitude as mean voltage (or area) in a broad window chosen in advance, and latency with fractional-area or 50%-area measures rather than peaks.
Report the reference. Avoid a Cz reference when measuring components with central maxima such as the P3 and ERN.
Space stimulus onsets about 1 s apart where possible and equate stimuli and ISIs across conditions, because early components are refractory.
Present visual stimuli briefly (about 200 ms or less) or long enough that offset responses do not overlap onset components.
Expect large differences between people in waveform shape, for example from differences in cortical folding.
Choose the electrode sites and time windows before analysing the data. ERP CORE recommends them for seven components in young adults; other groups may need adjustments.
Exclude participants with artifacts on more than 25% of trials, accuracy below 75%, or fewer than half the trials left in any condition, and report how many were excluded for each task.
Report the noise level of your data, such as the standard deviation of the voltage in the baseline, so it can be compared with ERP CORE's values.

measures.name: Auditory brainstem responses (waves I–VI)
measures.spec: Very early waves within about 10 ms of a brief sound, generated in the brainstem, before the middle-latency and cortical components.
measures.windowNote: First ~10 ms on Woodman's log-time plot (Fig. 2)

measures.name: Alpha power (8–12 Hz)
measures.spec: Power of the 8–12 Hz alpha rhythm, which dominates the raw EEG.

caveats.t: The largest noise source for early ERPs; it grows when participants are sleepy or bored.

methods.t: Jitter the intertrial interval so alpha does not phase-lock to the stimulation rate.

measures.name: C1
measures.spec: The first visual ERP deflection, peaking about 50–70 ms after a visual stimulus.

caveats.t: Small, overlaps the P1 and shares the frequency range of alpha noise, so a good individual measure can need over 1,000 artifact-free trials per condition.

measures.sitesNote: Occipitotemporal sites in Woodman's Fig. 1; no electrodes named

measures.name: Contralateral delay activity (CDA / SPCN)
measures.spec: Sustained posterior negativity contralateral to the remembered items during the retention interval of a lateralized visual working-memory task.

caveats.t: Individual differences in ERP amplitude can come from cortical folding and skull properties; the CDA is an example where they also track a cognitive ability.

measures.sitesNote: Posterior, contralateral versus ipsilateral; electrodes not named

measures.name: Contingent negative variation (CNV)
measures.spec: Slow negative shift that builds up before a stimulus the participant must respond to; includes orienting (O) and expectancy (E) waves.

caveats.t: In studies of stimulus-evoked activity, anticipatory activity like the CNV can differ between trial types and contaminate the baseline; randomize trial types and baseline-correct.

measures.windowNote: Before the imperative stimulus (no window given in the sources)

feasibility.note: Builds up before a stimulus that requires a response.

measures.name: Cortical Somatosensory evoked potentials
measures.sitesNote: P50 arises mainly from primary somatosensory cortex, P100/N140 from S2, P3b from distributed attention/updating networks.

measures.name: Error-related negativity (ERN/Ne) and feedback negativity (FBN)
measures.spec: Medial frontal negativity within about 100 ms after an incorrect response, with a broad, centrally maximal distribution; the feedback negativity follows feedback.

setup.t: ERP CORE task: a flanker task. A central arrow is flanked by arrows pointing the same way or the opposite way, and participants press a left- or right-hand button for the direction of the central arrow.
Re-reference offline to the average of P9 and P10, next to the mastoids.

caveats.t: A Cz reference shrinks components with central maxima such as the ERN.

methods.t: ERP CORE analysed the ERN only for participants with at least 6 error trials left after artifact rejection.

quantify.t: ERP CORE: mean amplitude of the incorrect-minus-correct difference wave at FCz, 0–100 ms after the response, with a −400 to −200 ms baseline.

measures.sitesNote: Medial frontal, broad with central maxima; electrodes not named

measures.name: High-beta/alpha ratio (resting state)
measures.spec: Ratio of high-beta (20–35 Hz) to alpha (8–12 Hz) amplitude, each normalized as % of the 0.488–100 Hz spectrum; eyes-open resting EEG, FFT on 2,048-ms epochs, averaged within ROIs
measures.sitesNote: Four 5-electrode ROIs: anterior left (F9, F7, FT7, F3, FC3), anterior right (F10, F8, FT8, F4, FC4), posterior left (CP3, P3, P7, TP7, O1), posterior right (CP4, P4, P8, TP8, O2); 38-channel 10–20 cap

measures.name: Lateralized readiness potential (LRP)
measures.spec: Difference wave: voltage at sites contralateral minus ipsilateral to the responding hand, developing before the response.

setup.t: ERP CORE task: a flanker task. A central arrow is flanked by arrows pointing the same way or the opposite way, and participants press a left- or right-hand button for the direction of the central arrow.
Re-reference offline to the average of P9 and P10, next to the mastoids.

quantify.t: ERP CORE: mean amplitude of the contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference at C3/C4 from 100 ms before the button press to the press itself, with a −800 to −600 ms baseline.

measures.sitesNote: C3 and C4: the side opposite the response hand minus the same side
measures.windowNote: Recommended by ERP CORE for its flanker task, time-locked to the button press

measures.name: Mismatch Negativity (MMN)

setup.t: ERP CORE task: a passive auditory oddball. Standard tones at 80 dB (80% of trials) and deviant tones at 70 dB (20%) play over speakers while participants watch a silent video and ignore the tones.
Re-reference offline to the average of P9 and P10, next to the mastoids.

quantify.t: MMN latencies and amplitudes extracted from the largest negativity occurring between 0 and 350 msec at Fz in the MMN waveform.
ERP CORE: mean amplitude of the deviants-minus-standards difference wave at FCz, 125–225 ms after the tone, with a −200 to 0 ms baseline.

measures.sitesNote: Fz in Cheng et al. (2025); FCz in ERP CORE, where the difference was largest
measures.windowNote: Recommended by ERP CORE; Cheng et al. (2025) took the largest negativity between 0 and 350 ms

measures.name: Visual N1 / N170 (N100)
measures.spec: Negative deflection peaking about 170–200 ms, with posterior and anterior subtypes; the N170 is the face-sensitive variant.

setup.t: ERP CORE task for the face-specific N170: pictures of faces, cars, scrambled faces and scrambled cars, one at a time at the centre of the screen; participants judge whether each is an object or a texture.
For the N170, re-reference offline to the average of all electrodes, the usual choice for this component.

caveats.t: Same physical stimulus confound as the P1: attended and unattended conditions must use the same stimuli.
Refractory at short interstimulus intervals; Woodman's rule of thumb is to space onsets about 1 s apart.

quantify.t: ERP CORE (N170): mean amplitude of the faces-minus-cars difference wave at PO8, 110–150 ms after the picture, with a −200 to 0 ms baseline.

measures.sitesNote: Posterior (occipitotemporal) for the posterior N1; no electrodes named

measures.name: N2 (N2 family)
measures.spec: Negative deflection peaking about 225–250 ms; a family of subcomponents (N2a, N2b, N2c, N2pc) that share polarity and timing but reflect different processes.

setup.t: Record EEG using scalp electrodes positioned according to the international 10–20 system, with the nose as the reference. Measure auditory N2 responses at the vertex electrode (Cz).

caveats.t: Overlaps the larger P3: an apparent N2 change can be an earlier P3 onset. Use scalp distribution to tell them apart.

lookFor.t: Identify the N2 peak through visual inspection of the auditory evoked potential waveform recorded at Cz.

measures.sitesNote: Measured at the vertex (Cz), with EEG recordings referenced to the nose.

measures.name: N2pc (PCN)
measures.spec: Contralateral-minus-ipsilateral negativity at occipitotemporal sites about 200 ms after a lateralized target appears among distractors.

setup.t: ERP CORE task: simple visual search. Each block has a target colour (pink or blue), and participants report whether the gap in the square of that colour is at the top or the bottom.
Re-reference offline to the average of P9 and P10, next to the mastoids.

caveats.t: Eye movements toward the target shift both the corneoretinal potential and the visual input; exclude them (EOG, and an eye tracker for absolute fixation).
ERP CORE also removed trials with horizontal eye movements larger than 0.2° of visual angle between −50 and 350 ms, because these could affect the N2pc.

methods.t: About 250 trials per condition per participant.

quantify.t: ERP CORE: mean amplitude of the contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference at PO7/PO8, 200–275 ms after the search array, with a −200 to 0 ms baseline.

measures.sitesNote: Occipitotemporal, contralateral minus ipsilateral to the target; electrodes not named

measures.name: N400
measures.spec: A negative-going wave that is larger for a word unrelated in meaning to the word before it than for a related word, from about 200 to 600 ms and largest over central-parietal midline sites.

setup.t: ERP CORE task: word pairs. A prime word is followed by a target word, and participants judge whether the two are related in meaning.
Re-reference offline to the average of P9 and P10, next to the mastoids.

quantify.t: ERP CORE: mean amplitude of the unrelated-minus-related difference wave at CPz, 300–500 ms after the target word, with a −200 to 0 ms baseline.

measures.sitesNote: Measured at CPz, where the difference was largest
measures.windowNote: The recommended window; the difference itself lasted from about 184 to 750 ms

measures.name: Visual P1 (P100)
measures.spec: Positive deflection about 90–100 ms after a visual stimulus as information moves through the visual system.

caveats.t: Physically different stimuli change P1 amplitude on their own; attention effects can only be claimed when the same stimuli contribute to attended and unattended conditions.
Needs roughly 300–1,000 trials per condition to measure reliably because it overlaps alpha-band noise.
Waveform shape varies widely across healthy individuals, likely from cortical folding and skull differences rather than processing.

measures.sitesNote: Occipitotemporal sites in Woodman's Fig. 1; no electrodes named

measures.name: P3 / P300 (P3a, P3b)
measures.spec: Large positive wave (often over 10 µV) with a broad central-to-parietal maximum; frontally distributed P3a versus centroparietal P3b.

setup.t: ERP CORE task: an active visual oddball. The letters A to E appear in random order, each on 20% of trials; one letter is the target in each block, so the same letter is a target in some blocks and a non-target in others.
Re-reference offline to the average of P9 and P10, next to the mastoids.

caveats.t: Do not use a Cz reference for components with central maxima such as the P3.

methods.t: About 35–60 trials per condition per participant are usually enough.
Not reduced at about 1 s interstimulus intervals, unlike the auditory N1 and P2.
ERP CORE measured the P3 at Pz because it is the most widely used site; CPz gave a similar amplitude.

quantify.t: ERP CORE: mean amplitude of the rare-minus-frequent difference wave at Pz, 300–600 ms after the letter, with a −200 to 0 ms baseline.

measures.sitesNote: Broad, central to centroparietal maximum (P3b); frontal for P3a
measures.windowNote: Recommended by ERP CORE for its letter oddball task

measures.name: Error positivity (Pe)
measures.spec: Positive deflection after errors, following the ERN.

constructs.name: Cognitive control and mental effort

aspects.name: Cognitive load
aspects.definition: Demand placed on limited processing resources.

constructs.definition: Top-down regulation of processing, and the demand a task places on limited resources.

constructs.name: Early auditory processing

aspects.name: Brainstem transmission
aspects.definition: The earliest neural responses to sound, generated in the brainstem within about 10 ms.

constructs.definition: The first stages of processing sound, from the brainstem to auditory cortex.

constructs.name: Early visual and sensory processing

aspects.name: First visual responses
aspects.definition: The first feedforward sweep of visual information through visual cortex.

constructs.definition: The first, largely automatic stages of processing what we see and sense.

aka: Conscious or affective evaluation of performance
constructs.name: Performance monitoring

aspects.name: Error detection
aspects.definition: Registering that a response was wrong.

aspects.name: Conscious or affective evaluation
aspects.definition: Awareness of, or an affective reaction to, one's own performance.

constructs.definition: Noticing errors, conflict between responses, and feedback, so that behaviour can be adjusted.

constructs.name: Preparing a response

aspects.name: Anticipation
aspects.definition: Cognitive and motor preparation for an expected stimulus that requires a response.

aspects.name: Response selection
aspects.definition: Choosing which response to make and preparing it.

constructs.definition: Getting ready for an expected event and preparing which response to make.

constructs.name: Recognizing and categorizing what you see

aspects.name: Object categorization
aspects.definition: Recognizing what an object is and assigning it to a category.

aspects.name: Faces and expert objects
aspects.definition: Recognizing faces and objects of expertise.

aspects.name: Stimulus evaluation
aspects.definition: Evaluating a stimulus and deciding which category it belongs to.

constructs.definition: Identifying objects and faces, and sorting stimuli into categories.

constructs.name: Selective attention

aspects.name: Covert visual attention
aspects.definition: Shifting attention to a peripheral target without moving the eyes.

aspects.name: Early (sensory-level) selection
aspects.definition: Attention changing sensory processing within the first ~100 ms, as early-selection models propose.

constructs.definition: Focusing on what the task needs by boosting the relevant input and suppressing the rest.

constructs.name: Semantic processing
constructs.definition: Processing the meaning of words. The paper on the site studies it by comparing a word that is related in meaning to the word before it with one that is not.

constructs.name: Vigilance and alertness
constructs.definition: How alert or drowsy a participant is.

constructs.name: Working memory

aspects.name: Visual maintenance
aspects.definition: Holding visual information in working memory over a short delay.

aspects.name: Context updating
aspects.definition: Revising the current representation of the task context when a relevant event occurs.

aspects.name: Controlling access
aspects.definition: Keeping irrelevant stimuli from being stored.

aspects.name: Visual capacity
aspects.definition: How much visual information an individual can store at once.

constructs.definition: Holding a small amount of information in mind for a few seconds, updating it, and the limits on how much can be held.

entries.cites: Walter et al. (1964); Brunia, van Boxtel & Böcker (in press)
entries.claim: Listed as the component that precedes a stimulus, indexing anticipation and cognitive and motor preparation; described as the first cognitive ERP component found once averaging became available.
entries.paradigm: A stimulus that requires a response, after a preparation period

entries.cites: Clark, Fan & Hillyard (1995); Jeffreys & Axford (1972); Zhang & Luck (2008)
entries.claim: Reflects sensory processing at about 50–70 ms; thought to arise in primary visual cortex and assumed to be wholly or mainly feedforward.

entries.cites: Heinze et al. (1994); Luck (1995); Vogel & Luck (2000)
entries.claim: Reflects sensory and perceptual processing at about 90–100 ms as information moves through the visual system; assumed to be largely feedforward.
Many studies report P1 and N1 modulations when attention is allocated to locations and stimuli, provided the same stimuli contribute to attended and unattended conditions.
entries.paradigm: Spatial or feature-based attention with stimuli counterbalanced across conditions

entries.claim: N1 is modulated, like the P1, when attention is allocated to locations and stimuli, provided the stimuli are identical across attention conditions.
entries.paradigm: Spatial or feature-based attention with stimuli counterbalanced across conditions

entries.claim: N1 (about 170–200 ms) is linked to perceptual processing and visual discrimination.
entries.paradigm: Detection versus discrimination tasks

entries.claim: The N170 variant is face-sensitive and is linked to expert recognition.
entries.paradigm: Faces versus other objects

entries.cites: Folstein & Van Petten (2008); Pritchard, Shappell & Brandt (1991)
entries.claim: N2 (about 225–250 ms) is associated with object recognition and categorization; best treated as one of a family of N2 components.

entries.cites: Eimer (1996); Luck & Hillyard (1994a, 1994b); Cohen et al. (2009)
entries.claim: Indexes the deployment of covert attention to peripheral targets. Its timing (about 200 ms) and distribution suggest feedback from an attentional control structure.
entries.paradigm: Visual search with bilateral arrays

entries.claim: P3 is linked to stimulus evaluation time and categorization.
P3 is linked to context (working memory) updating; with the CDA it indexes working-memory encoding and maintenance.
Listed among the processes the P3 indexes: cognitive load.
The CDA (also called SPCN) indexes maintenance of information in visual working memory.
entries.paradigm: Lateralized visual working-memory task

entries.claim: CDA amplitude predicts an individual's ability to store information in visual working memory.
entries.paradigm: Lateralized visual working-memory task

entries.claim: CDA amplitude also predicts how well an individual avoids storing irrelevant stimuli.
entries.paradigm: Lateralized working-memory task with distractors

entries.claim: Indexes selection and preparation of the motor response.
entries.paradigm: Choice task with left- and right-hand responses

entries.cites: Falkenstein et al. (2000); Gehring et al. (in press)
entries.claim: A medial frontal negativity after the response, linked to error processing.
entries.paradigm: Speeded choice task with errors

entries.claim: Listed (with the feedback negativity) as a possible reinforcement-learning signal.
Listed as a possible response-conflict signal.
Listed as reflecting affective or conscious assessment of task performance.
Auditory stimuli elicit very early waves, generated in the brainstem, before the middle-latency and cortical components.
entries.paradigm: Brief auditory stimulus; Cz; log-time plot

entries.claim: Alpha dominates the EEG, is particularly large when observers are sleepy or bored, and decreases when a stimulus appears; it is the largest noise source for early visual ERPs.

Implanted children had larger VEP amplitudes and earlier latencies, with right temporal cortex (including auditory regions) activated, which the authors read as visual cross-modal re-organization. N1 latency was negatively related to speech perception in background noise in the implanted group.

Researchers recorded brain activity (EEG) in 66 adults aged 53 to 80 while they watched two simple animations: an abstract shape and a cartoon talking mouth. They wanted to see whether the aging brain makes up for hearing loss by boosting vision. In people with worse hearing, a later stage of visual processing ran faster, while getting older on its own slowed it down. Their hearing regions also pitched in to help process the abstract shape, showing the aging brain can still rewire itself. The very first responses to the talking mouth were slower, though, possibly because seeing speech relies partly on hearing circuits. The brain adapts to hearing loss in some ways, but processing of speech-r
entries.paradigm: Passive VEP w apparent motion
entries.specUsed: Electrodes: Pz, P4, POz, O1, Oz, O2, M2, M1

entries.claim: Researchers observed differences in N2 amplitude between children with cochlear implants and normal-hearing children when processing vocal sounds. These findings suggest that auditory deprivation and cochlear implantation may influence cortical processing of human vocalizations, however the functional significance of N2 remains uncertain.
entries.paradigm: Listening to vocal sounds (laughing, coughing, sighing) and nonvocal environmental sounds
entries.population: 16 children, ~4–12 years old: 8 children with cochlear implants and 8 normal-hearing children

entries.claim: Used MMN to assess auditory information processing in children with congenital deafness following gene therapy or cochlear implantation. MMN latencies were significantly shorter in the gene-therapy group at 6 months and in the combined gene-therapy/cochlear implant group at 12 months compared with the comparison groups. This suggests that there are differences in neural auditory processing after hearing restoration.
entries.paradigm: Passive auditory standard-versus-deviant stimulus used to elicit MMN. MMN was assessed at postoperative follow-ups of 3, 6, and 12 months.
entries.behaviour: Auditory and speech perception assessed using IT-MAIS/MAIS, CAP, SIR, speech perception tests in quiet and noisy settings, and music perception measures.
entries.sitesNote: MMN latency and amplitude were extracted at the Fz electrode (Figure 4)
entries.population: 72 participants (1-18 years old) with congenital hearing loss; 11 gene-therapy recipients and 61 cochlear implant recipients.

entries.claim: In 92 adults aged 18–86 (passive auditory oddball with tone sequences), MMN amplitude shrank with age. Smaller MMNs went with poorer mnemonic discrimination of similar tone-sequence lures on a surprise recognition test, so the MMN, an index of early auditory change detection and encoding, predicted age-related declines in memory precision.
entries.paradigm: Passive auditory oddball with standard and deviant tone sequences (encoding), then a surprise old/new/similar recognition test with targets, similar lures and dissimilar foils
entries.behaviour: Mnemonic discrimination (lure discrimination index) and old/new recognition of tone sequences
entries.sitesNote: Mean of a 7-electrode frontal/frontocentral cluster (AFz, F1, Fz, F2, FC1, FCz, FC2), 200–400 ms after tone onset; average reference; 66-channel BioSemi 10–20 montage
entries.population: 92 healthy adults aged 18–86 (47 female): young, middle-aged and older adults

entries.claim: In older adults, MMNs to sound-location changes appeared for 10° shifts near the midline but, at lateral positions, only for 20° shifts toward the midline. MMN amplitude did not scale with the size of the shift (unlike in young adults), which the authors take as a sign of weaker pre-attentive encoding of sound-source location with age.
entries.paradigm: Passive free-field auditory oddball: noise-burst standards at +5° (central) or ±65° (lateral) azimuth, with rare deviants shifted 10° or 20° left or right
entries.behaviour: Compared against behavioural minimum audible angle (MAA) thresholds for sound localization
entries.sitesNote: MMN measured at Fz (peak 100–250 ms, mean of ±10 ms around peak); hemispheric comparison averaged F1/F3/F5/FC1/FC3/FC5 vs F2/F4/F6/FC2/FC4/FC6; 58 channels, nose-tip reference, ground at Fpz
entries.population: 15 older adults aged 65–82 (7 women), MMSE 27–30, audiometrically screened

entries.claim: After working memory training, older adults showed a higher resting high-beta/alpha ratio (taken as greater cortical arousal) over anterior, especially left frontal, sites than an active control group, still present at 6-month follow-up. Frontal ratios tracked better post-training working memory span and, at follow-up, fewer intrusion errors in the trained group only.
entries.paradigm: 3-min eyes-open resting EEG before and after working memory training and at 6-month follow-up, each followed by the Categorization Working Memory Span (CWMS) task; double-blind RCT vs active control
entries.behaviour: CWMS accuracy (working memory span) and CWMS intrusion errors (inhibitory control)
entries.sitesNote: Four 5-electrode ROIs: anterior left (F9, F7, FT7, F3, FC3), anterior right (F10, F8, FT8, F4, FC4), posterior left (CP3, P3, P7, TP7, O1), posterior right (CP4, P4, P8, TP8, O2); 38-channel 10–20 cap
entries.population: 24 healthy older adults aged 64–75, randomized to training or active control group

entries.claim: In a flanker task, incorrect responses produced a larger negativity than correct ones over midline frontocentral sites just after the response. The ERN is isolated as the incorrect-minus-correct difference, time-locked to the response.
entries.paradigm: Flanker task: a central arrow flanked by arrows pointing the same or the opposite way; left- or right-hand button press
entries.specUsed: Incorrect minus correct at FCz, 0–100 ms after the response
entries.population: 40 neurotypical young adults aged 18–30 from the UC Davis community; 36 kept for this component after exclusions

entries.claim: In a flanker task with left- and right-hand responses, the voltage over motor cortex opposite the responding hand became more negative than over the same side just before the response. The LRP is isolated as the contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference, time-locked to the response.
entries.paradigm: Flanker task: a central arrow flanked by arrows pointing the same or the opposite way; left- or right-hand button press
entries.specUsed: Contralateral minus ipsilateral at C3/C4, 100–0 ms before the response
entries.population: 40 neurotypical young adults aged 18–30 from the UC Davis community; 37 kept for this component after exclusions

entries.claim: In a passive auditory oddball, rare deviant tones produced a negativity peaking near 200 ms, largest over midline frontocentral sites. The MMN is isolated as the deviants-minus-standards difference wave.
entries.paradigm: Passive auditory oddball: standard tones at 80 dB (80%) and deviant tones at 70 dB (20%) while watching a silent video
entries.specUsed: Deviants minus standards at FCz, 125–225 ms after the tone
entries.population: 40 neurotypical young adults aged 18–30 from the UC Davis community; 39 kept for this component after exclusions

entries.claim: In a face-perception task, the N170 was larger and earlier for faces than for cars, largest over the right inferior temporal region. It is isolated as the faces-minus-cars difference wave.
entries.paradigm: Face perception: pictures of faces, cars, scrambled faces and scrambled cars; participants judge object or texture
entries.specUsed: Faces minus cars at PO8, 110–150 ms after the picture
entries.population: 40 neurotypical young adults aged 18–30 from the UC Davis community; 37 kept for this component after exclusions

entries.claim: In a simple visual search task, the voltage over the hemisphere opposite the target was more negative than over the same side from about 200 to 300 ms. The N2pc is isolated as the contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference.
entries.paradigm: Simple visual search: find the square in the target colour and report whether its gap is at the top or bottom
entries.specUsed: Contralateral minus ipsilateral at PO7/PO8, 200–275 ms after the search array

entries.claim: In a word-pair task, a second word unrelated in meaning to the first produced a larger negativity than a related word, from about 200 to 600 ms and largest over central-parietal midline sites. The N400 is isolated as the unrelated-minus-related difference.
entries.paradigm: Word-pair judgment: a prime word then a target word; participants judge whether they are related in meaning
entries.specUsed: Unrelated minus related at CPz, 300–500 ms after the target word
entries.population: 40 neurotypical young adults aged 18–30 from the UC Davis community; 39 kept for this component after exclusions

entries.claim: In an active visual oddball, letters from the rare target category produced a larger positive wave than frequent letters, largest at the parietal midline. The P3 is isolated as the rare-minus-frequent difference, and the same letter served as target and non-target in different blocks.
entries.paradigm: Active visual oddball: letters A to E, each on 20% of trials, with one letter as the target in each block
entries.specUsed: Rare minus frequent at Pz, 300–600 ms after the letter
entries.population: 40 neurotypical young adults aged 18–30 from the UC Davis community; 34 kept for this component after exclusions
